title: Data Serialization and Formatting
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose and key terms of data serialization and formatting.
Apply null representation in a small PostgreSQL-oriented example or design decision.
Validate the result against the expected behavior and identify one portability, safety, or edge-case consideration.

content.intro: Learn data serialization and formatting through a short explanation, a concept diagram, and a PostgreSQL-oriented example. Focus on the reason for the query or design decision before memorizing syntax.
content.why_it_matters: Data Serialization and Formatting matters because database behavior becomes more reliable when the intended row meaning, data shape, and edge cases are explicit. This lesson follows the SQL curriculum's listed subtopics and calls out PostgreSQL-specific behavior when it matters.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: A safe data serialization and formatting workflow separates ingestion from trusted production tables. Load into staging, validate encodings and data quality, reconcile counts, then apply well-defined changes in a transaction or restartable batch.

content_blocks.title: Apply the idea
content_blocks.text: Start with the subtopics: NULL representation, Date and time formats, Decimal and numeric formatting, Text encoding. Define the result you expect, run or inspect the small example in your own disposable PostgreSQL lab, and change one assumption at a time. The embedded lesson editor is a demonstration shell: the current project shows the sample expected output and does not execute arbitrary SQL on the server.

items.title: NULL representation
items.text: NULL representation requires deliberate handling of absent or unknown values. In SQL, NULL is not the same as zero or an empty string; use IS NULL / IS NOT NULL for direct tests and check how expressions and aggregates propagate unknowns.

items.title: Date and time formats
items.text: Date and time formats needs a clearly defined time zone and calendar grain. Prefer typed date/time values over formatted strings, define inclusive/exclusive boundaries, and check daylight-saving or month-boundary cases where they matter.

items.title: Decimal and numeric formatting
items.text: Decimal and numeric formatting works best when inputs and outputs have deliberate types. Use explicit casts when intent is unclear, guard against overflow or truncation, and avoid converting typed values to display strings before calculations finish.

items.title: Text encoding
items.text: Text encoding depends on text representation, collation, wildcard semantics, and sometimes locale. Test spaces, case, accents, Unicode, and special characters rather than assuming every database compares strings identically.

items.title: Escaping data values
items.text: Escaping data values helps you move data through staging, bulk load/export, encoding checks, validation, cleansing, and incremental synchronization workflows. Start with a concrete example, state the expected result, and verify the behavior before extending the query or design.

items.title: Consistent import/export conventions
items.text: Consistent import/export conventions helps you move data through staging, bulk load/export, encoding checks, validation, cleansing, and incremental synchronization workflows. Start with a concrete example, state the expected result, and verify the behavior before extending the query or design.

content_blocks.code: SELECT row_to_json(p) AS product_json FROM (SELECT product_id, name, price FROM products ORDER BY product_id LIMIT 3) AS p;
content_blocks.expected_output: The query serializes each selected product row as JSON text; JSON serialization does not itself validate business meaning or make data safe to expose.

content_blocks.reset_steps: For queries, restore the original text and compare results. For statements that change data, use the transaction and rollback shown in the example, or recreate the disposable lab from the included setup instructions. Do not reset production data.

content_blocks.title: Remember
content_blocks.text: SQL correctness depends on data shape, constraints, NULL behavior, row counts, and the target database dialect—not just whether a statement parses.

Inspect one edge case: missing values, duplicate matches, tied sort values, a constraint violation, or an engine-specific syntax difference.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming a query is correct because it returns some rows.
common_mistakes.why: A result can omit valid records, multiply joined rows, mishandle NULLs, or rely on a non-deterministic order.
common_mistakes.fix: Check the expected row grain, add targeted edge cases, and use a stable tie-breaker whenever order or pagination matters.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying PostgreSQL syntax into another SQL engine without checking support.
common_mistakes.why: PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, SQL Server, and Oracle differ in types, functions, row limits, procedural features, and transaction behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: Label the target engine/version and verify the relevant official reference before adapting the query.

common_mistakes.problem: Testing with production data or credentials.
common_mistakes.why: Practice statements can change rows or expose sensitive information if run against the wrong connection.
common_mistakes.fix: Use a dedicated disposable lab, check current_database() and current_user, and review all changes before committing.

summary: Data Serialization and Formatting is about making the database behavior and the expected result explicit.
Use the provided subtopics as a review checklist and validate a small test case.
